results.summary: This design generates two square waves: channel 0 with independently programmable high and low times, and channel 1 as a phase-shifted replica with a programmable delay. It is controlled over SPI by an external master such as an RP2350, which writes configuration registers; an encoder can also be used for fast-scan adjustments. The outputs are intended to be observed on an oscilloscope and can drive an SR latch for metastability experiments by bringing the two edges arbitrarily close. The design is notable for its specific focus on metastability exploration and its use of a Digilent PModEnc for interactive control.

This project implements a number-based memory game where the player must remember and submit sequences of numbers. It uses input switches for starting the game and submitting answers, with LED outputs to display game state and feedback. The documentation is very thin, providing only a one-line description and pin names, so the exact gameplay mechanics and display method are not fully specified. It appears to be a simple educational or demonstration project with no external hardware required beyond the PCB board's switches and LEDs.

BIST-8 implements a built-in self-test architecture for an 8-bit carry-lookahead adder, including a 12-bit LFSR pattern generator, a 16-bit MISR response compactor, fault injection, and a 4-state FSM controller. In normal mode it acts as a standard adder; in BIST mode it runs 4095 test vectors and compares the MISR signature against a golden value of 0xCF77. A fault injection input forces a stuck-at-0 fault on bit 3 of the adder output, producing a faulty signature of 0x927F to demonstrate detection. The design is notable for its complete self-test capability and clear documentation of expected signatures.

This design simulates a universal one-qubit quantum computer, executing operations such as reset, X/Y/Z/H/S/T gates, and measurement. Amplitudes are stored as 8-bit fixed-point numbers, and an LFSR provides pseudorandom numbers for measurement. The operation is selected via three input pins, and a start signal triggers execution; measurement results appear on an output pin, and a done signal indicates completion. The design is notable for bringing quantum computing concepts to a tiny digital chip, though it is limited to a single qubit.

This project implements a 2x2 systolic processing-element grid for CNN inference, controlled entirely over UART from a host PC. The host sends 3-byte packets to drive activations and weights, and receives 2-byte partial-sum results. It is tested using a Python host script that runs nine test cases matching the simulation testbench. The design requires a USB-to-UART adapter and a host PC, and is notable for its compact systolic architecture and UART-based control.

The Tiny Pixel Processor is a custom processor designed to procedurally generate graphics, outputting a 640x480 VGA signal with an internal resolution of 64x48 pixels. It features a 16-bit custom instruction set and 8 registers, and can be programmed via UART using a provided Python script. The default configuration runs a simple program that generates a procedural pattern, which can be displayed on a VGA monitor using the tiny-vga board. The design is notable for its application-specific architecture and the ability to upload new programs over UART.

This project implements a compact 32-bit RISC-V processor with a five-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB). It includes two UART interfaces (one for bootloading, one for general communication), an SPI master interface, and GPIO pins. The design is intended for hardware deployment and can be tested via simulation and on an FPGA or ASIC. It is notable for being a zero-to-ASIC demo project, showcasing a complete RISC-V core with standard peripherals.

This design implements an RGB mixer that uses two push buttons (inc and dec) and a 2-position dip switch to select one of three PWM outputs. The selected output's pulse width is increased or decreased by the buttons, allowing control of the brightness of each RGB LED color. It requires external push buttons, a dip switch, an RGB LED, and resistors for pull-up configurations. The design is a custom implementation of the Z2A course's RGB mixer, intended for educational purposes.

BioPulse Tile processes an 8-bit radar or biosignal sample stream to detect breathing cycles, classify breathing patterns (normal, fast, slow, irregular, apnea), and detect heartbeats, all using digital logic without a CPU. It includes a demo mode with synthetic patterns, and streams metrics over UART. The design is tested with a cocotb testbench and can be used with external radar or biosignal front-ends. It is notable for its comprehensive vital-sign monitoring capabilities in a tiny digital tile.

This design is a GF180mcuD port of a ring-oscillator PVT sensor featuring five gatable ring oscillators with different stage counts, a 16-bit frequency counter, auto gate timer, prescaler, XOR jitter TRNG, per-RO health history, differential beat-frequency mode, and frequency-bounds health monitor. It supports both parallel and SPI control modes, with a register file for configuration and readout. The design is intended for cross-foundry PVT characterization and includes a cocotb test suite. It is notable for its comprehensive on-chip characterization features and the inclusion of GF-specific health-history registers.
